Modern distributed application architectures require a robust, decoupled approach to identity and access management, a challenge expertly solved by the intersection of OAuth2 and OpenID Connect (OIDC). In this ecosystem, OAuth2 acts as an authorization framework allowing third-party applications to obtain limited access to an HTTP service, while OIDC layers an identity protocol on top of OAuth2, introducing an ID token for user authentication. Understanding this landscape requires mastering specific core components: the Authorization Code grant, Client Credentials grant, and the Resource Server.

The Authorization Code grant is the gold standard for user-facing applications, relying on a back-channel exchange to protect sensitive tokens from interception by utilizing a short-lived authorization code that the client exchanges for tokens via a direct TLS connection with the authorization server. Conversely, the Client Credentials grant is strictly designed for machine-to-machine (M2M) communication where no user context exists, allowing a daemon or microservice to authenticate directly using its own client_id and client_secret to secure system-level APIs. Finally, the Resource Server is the component hosting the protected APIs; it does not issue tokens itself, but rather validates incoming JSON Web Tokens (JWTs) or introspects opaque tokens presented by clients, enforcing granular method- and endpoint-level security policies based on extracted scopes and authorities.

PKCE (Proof Key for Code Exchange) + Redirects

items: The Authorization Code flow requires PKCE (RFC 7636) even for confidential clients in modern Spring Security implementations to prevent authorization code interception attacks.

Resource Servers in Spring Security use Nimbus JOSE + JWT libraries under the hood to parse, verify cryptographic signatures against a remote JWK Set (JWKS), and map claims to Spring's GrantedAuthority collections via a JwtAuthenticationConverter.

Client Credentials flows leverage Spring's reactive or servlet WebClient combined with a ClientRegistrationRepository to automatically manage token acquisition, caching, and preemptive refresh cycles without polluting business logic.

parsed_answer.content: A classic production failure mode when deploying OAuth2 Resource Servers behind an API Gateway or Load Balancer is failing to configure X-Forwarded-* headers correctly. If the Resource Server attempts to fetch the JWKS URI via HTTP instead of HTTPS due to SSL termination at the gateway, signature verification will fail catastrophically or throw connection timeouts. Always ensure your gateway properly propagates proxy headers or explicitly override the issuer-uri and jwks-uri in your application properties.
